Map rundown−
Farmers plant seeds. Some of those seeds have had genes added in a laboratory — usually taken from bacteria — so the crop survives being sprayed with weedkiller when a field full of weeds is sprayed, or makes its own insecticide in every leaf and root. These are examples of Genetic Modification. The technique is fifty years old.

Proponents argue that, in the context of agriculture, insect-resistant cotton substantially reduced broad-spectrum insecticide spraying in several countries — sprays that killed bees, birds and farm workers — and the claim that these foods are unsafe to eat has not held up in decades of testing. But, that isn’t the whole story.

For one, seeds and pollen do not stay where you put them. In Oregon a grass engineered to survive weedkiller got out of its test fields; three years after the cleanup started, 62 of every 100 plants tested carried the gene, and it had crossed into two other grass species, one of them a different genus entirely. The product was pulled, the company was fined $500,000, and the grass is still out there. In North Dakota, researchers drove 3,000 miles testing roadside canola: more than 75% carried an engineered gene, and some carried two at once — a combination nobody bred, On the coast of Mexico grows the wild ancestor of cotton. In 2008 it carried no engineered genes. Ten years later, 60% of the plants tested did.

And spreading isn’t the end of it. Every wild plant sits inside a web of relationships with other species — things that guard it, feed on it, pollinate it, live in its roots, carry its seeds — and an engineered change entering at one point comes out at many others nobody has been watching or even defining. Wild plants carrying an engineered gene, for example, drew fewer of the insect species that defend them, and took the worst feeding damage of any group tested; parasitic wasps that control caterpillar numbers and that weren’t targeted in the first place came out 35% lighter after eating prey that carried the plant’s own built-in insecticide; introgressed wild cotton was found to hold less genetic variety than its unmodified neighbours, and Mexican wild cotton is now listed as vulnerable, with gene flow from crops being the main threat. Genetically modified insecticide-producing plants that travel beyond the field and cross-breed with wild plants also make less toxin than the original, leading to weaker doses of the plants’ insecticide, the exact conditions under which insect resistance to it spreads fastest.

Nobody knows the true ecological impacts of all of these combined. And, yet, some GMOs are released on purpose at enormous scale, as will be the case with gene drives, which are built specifically to push through entire wild populations by 2030. Engineered insects have been let loose by the hundred million, and engineered bacteria coated onto seed spread across millions of acres with nothing registered, as a microbe on a seed is not a plant, spraying it is not planting — no rule catches it.

Monitoring is thin enough that the clearest case was found only by accident; and the communities affected are rarely asked. In fact, people are sometimes contractually blocked from checking. In 2009, twenty-six university corn insect scientists told the US environment agency that the contracts attached to the seed did not permit them to run their own studies on crops already being sold. And, worst of all, containment has proven to fail, and spread is irreversible — there is no undoing it.

Four companies dominate the seed and chemical business: Bayer, Corteva, Syngenta and BASF. Roughly 94% of engineered crop area is just three crops — soy, maize and cotton — and 81% of it sits in three countries: the United States, Brazil and Argentina. Of 362 live US authorisations to release engineered organisms, Bayer, Syngenta and Pioneer hold 36% between them; Bayer alone holds 19%.

Bayer sells the seed that survives Roundup, and Bayer sells Roundup. The trait does not compete with the chemical business — it creates the market for it. One sale earns twice. This is why, even over 50 years, drought tolerance, better nutrition, higher yield haven’t been made, as they don’t sell a second product alongside the seed.

The seed is also patented, which matters because a patent covers the plant itself and everything grown from it. So the farmer signs a contract agreeing not to keep any of the harvest for next spring, and buys new seed every year instead of replanting what they already have. This means that saving seed isn’t merely a breach of contract but a crime. Ghana’s version of the seed-ownership treaty UPOV 91, for example, carries a ten-year minimum sentence. Nobody is liable either when that seed drifts: a neighbouring organic farm whose crop tests positive loses the certification its price depends on, and carries the loss itself

And, of course, the organisms themselves have no say in all of this. They are born simply because a company decided which trait would sell, and they are released into a world that had no part in the decision either.

Meanwhile, around forty countries have moved gene-edited organisms outside registration entirely. On April 30, 2025, the United States approved pigs edited to resist a disease that spreads in the crowded conditions of factory farms, an edit that raises antibiotic use by more than 200%. The animals are marketed with the claim that they are “not GMOs,” because their DNA was edited rather than supplemented with foreign DNA. In animal testing too, most laboratory animals are not legally animals. In the United States, mice, rats and birds bred for research are excluded from the Animal Welfare Act. They are the overwhelming majority of animals used, so the great bulk of the practice appears in no official count at all. Catalogues run to thousands of mouse strains, each one a line bred to be ill in a particular way, shipped to order. In pet cloning, dogs and horses are cloned for anyone who pays, and no biosafety rule applies, because nothing foreign was inserted and the rules only trigger on inserted material. If an industry can name its way out of the rulebook like this, there is no rulebook. And, when the referees themselves are part of the game — regulators, registers, patent offices and standards bodies —, not outside the industry checking it, who’s there to call their foul play?

And, even where regulation does exist, much of the evidence behind approvals comes from the companies themselves. Safety studies are usually commissioned and paid for by the manufacturer, while regulators primarily evaluate the reports that companies submit. There is no comprehensive public register of these studies, so outside researchers cannot tell which tests were conducted, which produced unfavorable results, or whether unsuccessful studies were simply repeated until a satisfactory outcome was obtained. Furthermore, a venture fund has to sell its stake within a fixed number of years, and that deadline rewards moving fast and getting big long before any regulator sees the product. These problems are not necessarily discovered at the regulator’s desk; they appear later in fields, hospitals, or ecosystems. This is not without precedent. In the 1970s, the testing company Industrial Bio-Test was found to have falsified safety data supporting thousands of pesticide approvals.

Meanwhile, use of the technology has become increasingly unpredictable. Although the repositories that distribute plasmids, cell lines, and other standard biological materials generally require verified institutional affiliations, many firms only voluntarily screen orders against databases of dangerous pathogen sequences. No law requires them to do so. The industry association responsible for this voluntary system has estimated that its members account for roughly 80 percent of global DNA synthesis, leaving about one-fifth of the market outside any screening process. A lock on four of five doors isn’t a lock. Anyone seeking prohibited sequences can therefore turn to an unscreened supplier, and because no record exists of who asked for what, nothing can be traced. This is how, in 2017, researchers reconstructed an extinct poxvirus for approximately $100,000.

Keep in mind that, under most national rules, contained laboratory and glasshouse work, as opposed to anything put into a field, a river or a patient, only needs the facility registered once and the risk class recorded internally. Within that, a laboratory can create novel organisms that have never existed, insert genes across kingdoms, build gene drives, resurrect viral sequences, and run it at industrial fermenter scale — without any per-experiment approval, public notice, or entry in any register — building essentially any organism, at any scale, indefinitely, under the radar. The reporting trigger is almost always only upon release, not creation. The UK is the strictest and even there it’s a notification to the HSE with no public file. The EU requires a one-time facility notification. The US has no statutory contained-use requirement at all — NIH guidelines bind only institutions taking federal money, and enforcement is a local committee whose records aren’t public. That is the same permission under which, in 2011, two laboratories took an avian influenza that killed a large share of the people it infected and could not pass between them, and made it transmissible between ferrets — the standard model for human transmission. Contained work, so no approval for the experiment and no public notice; the world learned of it when the papers were submitted. And in 2005 a team rebuilt the 1918 influenza virus, which had killed tens of millions and no longer existed, from sequenced fragments. Both were lawful throughout, both were published, and the argument happened afterwards — producing review rules that apply only to work the government pays for.

No amount of good intent at one end can change what has become buildable at the other. We sit on a precipice.

This map is the industry behind all of this — the companies that design and sell engineered organisms, the ones supplying them with DNA, animals and laboratory capacity, the money behind them, and the bodies that authorise them and argue on their behalf. Four hundred and thirty-six organisations, each with its own write-up and a link to the source. Twenty-four thousand release authorisations from official registers, broken down by country and state. Twenty-five documented cases of engineered organisms turning up where nobody put them. Two hundred regions that have declared themselves GMO-free. And thirty-six countries shaded by how each one decides what even counts as regulated.

Twelve facets, running the length of the chain: seed and traits, gene editing and synthetic biology, DNA synthesis and sequencing, contract research and manufacturing, laboratory animals, livestock and aquaculture and pets, insects and microbes and open release, de-extinction, human clinical work, assisted reproduction, the money, and the rules. A handful of companies write the DNA everything starts as. Hired laboratories run the studies regulators read. Breeders sell millions of engineered animals a year, catalogued like supplies. Ventures rebuild extinct species as intellectual property. Clinics consolidate human reproduction. Venture funds, public grants, philanthropies and defence agencies pay for all of it.

▾ Where this data comes from & what's not (yet) in it
Nearly everything here is state-published: biosafety law in most countries requires a public register, medicines regulators publish trial sponsors, and fertility regulators publish licensed clinics. Very little of it is published in a form a machine can read. That single fact shapes every layer on this map, and it is the reason the coverage is uneven in the particular ways set out below.

What is on the map, and where each layer came from.
• Releases — 22,163 records. Almost all from APHIS, which publishes two files updated each business day, in the public domain. Alongside them, 51 country records from the Biosafety Clearing-House and five Australian OGTR licences transcribed by hand.
• Facilities — 20,679 records. Fertility clinics from the national registers that publish one; animal facilities from USDA APHIS, the Canadian Council on Animal Care, AAALAC and Farm Transparency; maximum-containment laboratories from Global BioLabs.
• Clinical trials — 2,231 sponsors for gene and cell therapy, from the trial registries.
• Industry — 711 organisations, hand-built, because no register lists them.
• Regimes, treaties and zones, read from statutes and from the depositaries’ ratification lists rather than harvested from a feed.

What each layer leaves out, and why
• Releases are almost entirely American, and that is a publishing fact. APHIS is the only regulator on Earth that puts its whole register in a bulk file a machine can read — which is a different thing from publishing the most. EU member states publish trial locations to the municipality or the parcel under the deliberate release directive, and Australia’s OGTR holds more — every licence, every risk assessment, and site locations for active field trials — and disallows automated access in its robots.txt, so it has to be read by hand. The EU, Canada, Brazil, Argentina, India and New Zealand all hold real registers; none publishes a bulk file, most are search forms over a database, and several are PDF minutes.
• The Biosafety Clearing-House can be read after all. The register established under the Cartagena Protocol is the only genuinely cross-national record of its kind. Its website returns nothing to a fetcher, but the page fills itself from a search endpoint at api.cbd.int, and that endpoint answers. A harvester is written and waiting on a run; until then the country directory here comes from the Secretariat’s focal point list, published as a PDF.
• Contained laboratory work is under-recorded everywhere. Most of it is notified rather than licensed, and notifications are rarely published record by record. Every layer here will under-count how much engineering is happening relative to how much is released.
• Gene-edited organisms are increasingly outside registration. Where a jurisdiction has moved editing out of its registration requirement — around forty have — no record is created, so there is nothing to harvest. An absence of dots there means the law stopped requiring one. This is the largest structural gap on the map and it is growing.
• An edited organism cannot be followed from country to country. An organism made by inserting a gene from another species is issued an international serial number, and every regulator that rules on it files under that same string, which is why this map repeats the instruction to write the number down. An organism made by editing its own genes is issued nothing, because the identifier system was built around insertions. Canada’s register is the one harvestable place listing both kinds side by side: none of the 27 approved edited products carries an identifier, against 98 of the 101 inserted ones.
• Facilities are a patchwork, and the pattern is legal rather than technical. Fertility clinics are well covered where a regulator publishes a register — the UK, the US, China, India — and absent where none exists, which is most of the world. Animal research is thinner: the US and Canada publish registers, the UK publishes procedure counts without naming the establishment, and the EU publishes only totals. Maximum-containment laboratories have no register in any jurisdiction; the only global account is a research project, and it lists 69 BSL4 laboratories no government is obliged to declare. Where a register gives a mailing city rather than a street, the marker sits at that city and says so.
• Germline work, embryo selection and assisted reproduction are carried as clinics and sponsors. What is still absent is germline research itself, which no country requires to be registered publicly, and embryo screening, which happens inside those clinics and is reported by none of them.
• The industry layer is hand-built and will stay that way. No register lists the companies in this field, so every entry was found, read and written by hand. No facet is empty, but 711 organisations is not a census of an industry — read it as a map of its significant parts.
• Regulatory regimes are read from law. The 197 classifications come from statutes and Cartagena Protocol membership. Thirteen countries have no biosafety statute this map could find and are drawn as such. Forty-one dependencies are not classified at all, because they are governed under another country’s law: fifteen under the United Kingdom — Anguilla, Bermuda, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, the Falklands, Gibraltar, Guernsey, the Isle of Man, Jersey, Montserrat, Pitcairn, St Helena, South Georgia, the Turks and Caicos, the British Indian Ocean Territory; seven under France — French Polynesia, the French Southern Territories, New Caledonia, St Barthélemy, St Martin, St Pierre and Miquelon, Wallis and Futuna; six under the United States — American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Marianas, Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, the Minor Outlying Islands; three under the Netherlands — Aruba, Curaçao, Sint Maarten; three under New Zealand — the Cook Islands, Niue, Tokelau; two under Denmark — Greenland, the Faroes; two under Australia — Norfolk Island, Heard and McDonald; and one each under Norway (Svalbard and Jan Mayen), Finland (Åland) and Morocco (Western Sahara, disputed). A decision taken in London or Paris applies in places that never appear in a register of their own.
• Treaty membership is the one complete layer. Five treaties, every party drawn, from the depositaries’ own ratification lists. A country that is not shaded is not a party.
• Ownership is only what the registers admit. Where a regulator names a parent company, that is recorded; where a chain simply trades under one name across a dozen sites, that is recorded as an inference. Share registers are not here: who actually owns these businesses sits in company filings across dozens of jurisdictions, and reading those is a separate project.
